title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 46–47 (editorial revision)
description: Units 46–47 editorially checked against teaching pages, illustrations, exercises and answer key. Coverage focuses on phrasal verbs, distinct senses, object placement, everyday routines, frequency, transport and time. Original example sentences, Brazilian Portuguese translations and British English IPA.
sourceNotice: The supplied textbook was used to verify learning targets and contexts. All example sentences are original; textbook illustrations and exercises are not reproduced.

units.title: Unit 46 — Phrasal verbs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 46, textbook pp. 98–99 (PDF pp. 99–100); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.pt: verbo frasal; verbo acompanhado de partícula
items.example: “Get up” is a common phrasal verb.
items.note: A phrasal verb combines a verb and a particle. Together they may express a meaning different from the verb alone.

items.example: In “turn off”, “off” is the particle.
items.note: Up, on, off and down are particles used in this unit. Their meanings are not interchangeable; group phrasal verbs by topic when studying them.

items.example: I get up at seven on weekdays.
items.note: Past simple: got up. Get up means leave your bed; wake up means stop sleeping (also compared in Unit 47).

items.example: We got up early for the trip.
items.note: Get → got → got in the usual British English pattern. Got up is the past simple of get up.

items.pt: embarcar; subir (em ônibus, trem ou outro transporte)
items.example: Please get on before the bus leaves.
items.note: Use get on with a bus, train or coach. We normally say get in a car; that contrast is additional guidance.

items.example: We got on the bus near the park.
items.note: Use get on the bus, not get the bus on, when boarding a vehicle. Past simple: got on.

items.example: Get off at the last stop.
items.note: Get off is the opposite of get on when leaving a bus, train or coach. Past simple: got off.

items.example: They got off the train in the city centre.
items.note: Use get off the train, bus or coach to describe leaving that form of transport.

items.example: Could you turn on the kitchen light?
items.note: Separable: turn on the light = turn the light on. With a pronoun, say turn it on.

items.example: Turn off the television before you leave.
items.note: Separable: turn off the TV = turn the TV off. With a pronoun, say turn it off.

items.example: Please turn the radio up a little.
items.note: Here, turn up means make a device louder: turn up the radio, turn the radio up or turn it up.

items.pt: abaixar o volume; deixar mais baixo
items.example: The music is loud, so I will turn it down.
items.note: For volume, turn down is the opposite of turn up. Place a pronoun before the particle: turn it down.

items.example: Please go on; I want to hear the end of your story.
items.note: Past simple: went on. Go on + -ing means continue an activity; go on to do something has a different meaning.

items.example: The team went on working after dinner.
items.note: Use go on + -ing to describe continuing an activity. The exercise also practises went on working.

items.pt: ir embora; sair de um lugar
items.example: She went off before I could say goodbye.
items.note: In this unit, go off means leave a place. It has other meanings in different contexts.

items.pt: foi embora; saiu (passado de go off)
items.example: The visitors went off in a hurry.
items.note: Go → went → gone. In this context, went off means left or went away.

items.pt: vestir; colocar uma peça de roupa
items.example: Put on a jacket because it is cold.
items.note: Separable: put on your coat = put your coat on. The past simple of put is also put.

items.example: It is windy today, so put your coat on.
items.note: Put your coat on and put on your coat are both correct, as shown on the teaching page.

items.example: This coat is warm; put it on.
items.note: With a pronoun, use put it on, not put on it. This illustrates the separable pattern in an additional example.

items.example: Come on! The train is leaving.
items.note: A common informal expression of encouragement or urgency, especially when asking someone to hurry.

items.example: Turn on the oven before you prepare the meal.
items.note: The picture exercise applies turn on to an oven. Turn the oven on is also correct.

items.example: Please turn off the light when you leave.
items.note: Turn off the light = turn the light off. With a pronoun, say turn it off.

items.example: I cannot hear the news; turn the radio up.
items.note: The exercise reinforces turn up for higher volume; turn down is used for lower volume.

items.section: B · One phrasal verb, different meanings
items.example: I turned down the job because it was too far away.
items.note: This sense means refuse, unlike turn down meaning lower the volume. You can turn down an invitation or turn an invitation down.

items.section: B · One phrasal verb, different meanings
items.example: He turned down an invitation to the party.
items.note: Here, turn down means refuse. With a pronoun object, use turn it down.

items.section: B · One phrasal verb, different meanings
items.example: Our plane takes off at nine tomorrow.
items.note: An aircraft takes off when it leaves the ground. This use has no object. Past simple: took off.

items.section: B · One phrasal verb, different meanings
items.example: The plane took off late last night.
items.note: Take → took → taken. For aircraft, took off means left the ground.

items.section: B · One phrasal verb, different meanings
items.example: She took off her shoes at the door.
items.note: To remove clothing: take off your shoes = take your shoes off. With a pronoun, use take them off.

items.section: B · One phrasal verb, different meanings
items.example: Please take your shoes off before you enter.
items.note: Both take off your shoes and take your shoes off are grammatical; this alternative object order is additional usage guidance.

items.pt: abaixar o volume; recusar uma oferta ou convite, conforme o contexto
items.section: B · One phrasal verb, different meanings
items.example: If the offer is not right for you, turn it down.
items.note: With the pronoun it, the middle position is required. Context determines whether this means lower the volume or refuse something.

learningObjectives: Identify a phrasal verb as a verb plus a particle and interpret its meaning in context.
Use get up, get on/off, turn on/off/up/down, go on/off, put on and come on in everyday situations.
Distinguish the two taught senses of turn down (lower the volume/refuse) and take off (leave the ground/remove clothing).
Choose appropriate particles and place noun objects and pronoun objects correctly in separable phrasal verbs.
Recognise past forms such as got up/on/off, went off/on and took off; use go on + -ing for continued action.

units.title: Unit 47 — Everyday things
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 47, textbook pp. 100–101 (PDF pp. 101–102); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: I wake up at six but stay in bed for a few minutes.
items.note: Wake up means stop sleeping; get up means leave the bed. Past simple: woke up.

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: My brother gets up at half past seven.
items.note: Often follows wake up. Third-person singular in the present simple: gets up.

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: I go to the bathroom after I get up.
items.note: Go to the bathroom uses to to indicate direction.

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: She has a shower before breakfast.
items.note: A common British English collocation. Third-person singular: has a shower; past simple: had a shower.

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: We have breakfast together on Sundays.
items.note: Normally no article is needed when referring to the daily meal: have breakfast.

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: I listen to the radio while I make breakfast.
items.note: Listen takes to before its object: listen to the radio. Hear does not require to.

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: My sister goes to work by train.
items.note: When work refers to your usual destination, say go to work, normally without the.

items.pt: voltar para casa; chegar em casa
items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: I come home at six in the evening.
items.note: Home needs no to in this expression: come home. Past simple: came home.

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: We make dinner after work.
items.note: Make dinner refers to preparing a meal; have dinner refers to eating it.

items.pt: telefonar para um amigo; ligar para um amigo
items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: I phone a friend every Friday.
items.note: Phone is a transitive verb in this use: phone a friend, without to before the person.

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: She calls a friend after dinner.
items.note: Here, call means phone. Say call someone, not call to someone when you mean telephone them.

items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: They watch TV after dinner.
items.note: Watch TV describes the usual activity of watching television; the is normally omitted.

items.pt: ir dormir; ir para a cama
items.section: A · Things we do every day
items.example: The children go to bed at nine.
items.note: Go to bed means go to your bed to sleep; it contrasts with get up.

items.example: He washes clothes on Saturday morning.
items.note: Third-person singular: washes. Clothes ends in /ðz/ in standard British pronunciation.

items.example: We clean the house every weekend.
items.note: Clean the house or a room means make it clean; wash clothes refers to doing laundry.

items.pt: sair para caminhar; dar uma caminhada
items.example: I go for a walk in the park on Sundays.
items.note: A fixed expression meaning take a walk. Use for, not to, in this construction.

items.example: My grandfather writes letters to old friends.
items.note: Write → wrote → written. Letters here are written messages sent to another person.

items.example: She writes emails to her colleagues at lunchtime.
items.note: Singular: write an email. Plural: write emails. Write takes a direct object in these examples.

items.pt: sair de casa para lazer; sair
items.example: We go out with friends on Friday evenings.
items.note: In the source question How often do you go out?, this means leave home for social or leisure activities.

items.example: I watch a film at home every Saturday.
items.note: Film is common in British English. Watch takes a direct object, without to.

items.example: How often do you visit your friends?
items.note: Asks about frequency, not clock time. Answers can include every day, sometimes or three times a week.

items.example: How often do you go for a walk?
items.note: A question pattern for present routines: How often do you + base-form verb? The ellipsis is not spoken; speechText gives a complete example for TTS.

items.word: three or four times a week
items.pt: três ou quatro vezes por semana
items.example: I cook at home three or four times a week.
items.note: A frequency pattern: number + times + a week. Times counts how often an activity happens.

items.word: two or three times a week
items.pt: duas ou três vezes por semana
items.example: We phone our parents two or three times a week.
items.note: A frequency expression reinforced in Exercise 47.2. A week means per week.

items.example: What time do you finish work?
items.note: Asks for a clock time. When can ask for a time, day or general period.

items.word: What time do you get up?
items.pt: A que horas você se levanta?
items.example: What time do you get up on Sundays?
items.note: Questions about clock time are often answered with at: at seven, at about eight, etc.

items.example: When do you have dinner?
items.note: When asks for a time, day or period; What time focuses more specifically on clock time.

items.example: When do you have dinner at the weekend?
items.note: Exercise 47.2 practises questions with When and answers giving an approximate time.

items.pt: como; de que maneira (meio de transporte)
items.example: How do you travel to the city centre?
items.note: How asks about the way or means of travelling. How often asks about frequency.

items.word: How do you go to work?
items.pt: Como você vai para o trabalho?
items.example: How do you go to work when it rains?
items.note: A question about the means of transport. Possible answers are by bus, by train or by car.

items.example: He goes to work by bus.
items.note: Use by bus for the means of transport, without an article. On the bus refers to being aboard it.

items.example: My cousin travels to work by train.
items.note: Use by train, without an article, when describing the means of transport.

items.example: She usually goes to work by car.
items.note: Use by car for the means of transport, without an article; in the car means inside the vehicle.

items.example: I usually have breakfast at home.
items.note: A frequency adverb used before a main verb: I usually get up early. Do not use used to for a current habit.

items.example: We normally walk home after work.
items.note: Very close to usually in this context. It generally appears before a main verb.

items.example: Sometimes I write to my cousins.
items.note: May occur at the beginning of a sentence or before a main verb. It indicates a lower frequency than usually.

items.example: I go to work every day except Sunday.
items.note: Every day (two words) is a frequency expression. Everyday (one word) is an adjective.

items.example: He listens to the radio every morning.
items.note: Every + time period expresses regularity and normally needs no preposition.

items.example: She washes clothes every Saturday.
items.note: Do not add on before every Saturday. Compare on Saturday morning.

items.example: I clean my room on Saturday morning.
items.note: Use on with a named day, at with a clock time, and in with a general part of the day.

items.pt: à noite; no período da noite
items.example: I watch TV in the evening.
items.note: Use in the evening for this part of the day. In the evenings refers to repeated evenings and appears in Exercise 47.3.

items.pt: à noite; todas as noites; durante as noites (em uma rotina)
items.example: In the evenings, I usually read or watch TV.
items.note: This plural phrase describes an evening routine; it appears in Exercise 47.3 and contrasts with the singular in the evening.

items.example: I get up at seven o’clock on weekdays.
items.note: Use at for clock times. O’clock is used for whole hours, not for times such as 7.30.

items.pt: jantar; fazer a refeição do jantar
items.example: We have dinner at about eight.
items.note: Have dinner means eat the meal; make dinner means prepare it.

items.example: I usually have a cup of tea in the afternoon.
items.note: A common collocation for a drink. Use at when adding a specific clock time.

items.example: He has a cup of coffee before work.
items.note: Have is common with meals and drinks: have breakfast, have tea, have coffee.

items.example: I come home from work around five.
items.note: From indicates the starting point. Home needs no to. You can ask What time ...? or How ...? about the return journey.

items.example: My neighbour walks home after work.
items.note: Walk home describes the means of getting home. Do not add to before home.

items.example: I clean my room every weekend.
items.note: A variation of clean the house, practised in the routine questions in Exercise 47.2.

items.pt: ligar para seu melhor amigo ou sua melhor amiga
items.example: She phones her best friend twice a week.
items.note: Phone takes a direct person object and needs no preposition to.

items.example: I usually get up early, but yesterday I got up late.
items.note: Usually get up describes a present habit; got up is the past simple for a completed event. Used to describes a past habit, not a current one.

learningObjectives: Describe everyday activities, from waking up to going to bed.
Distinguish wake up from get up, make dinner from have dinner, and phone from call; use common routine collocations.
Describe occasional activities such as washing clothes, cleaning the house or a room, going for a walk and writing letters or emails.
Ask questions with How often, What time, When and How; answer using frequency expressions, times and transport.
Use usually, normally, sometimes, every day, time prepositions and by bus/train/car appropriately.
Distinguish a current habit with usually from a completed past event with got up; avoid using used to for present habits.
